question: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents with complaints of extra teeth in his lower and upper jaws. He was born by cesarean section at full term and his birth weight was 3.6 kg (7.9 lb). Until 6 months of age, he was breastfed and after that, solid foods were started. He did not cry immediately after birth, for which he was admitted to the intensive care unit where he also developed jaundice. There is a family history of intellectual disability. His motor milestones were delayed. His intelligence quotient (IQ) is 56. His temperature is 37.0ºC (98.6ºF), pulse is 88/min, and respiratory rate is 20/min. On physical examination, he has behavior disorders with autistic features, elongated face with large forehead, and prominent chin. His intraoral examination shows the presence of multiple teeth with crowding in both the upper and lower jaws, along with high arch palate and macroglossia. Genital examination reveals enlarged testicles. Panoramic radiographic examination shows teeth crowding in the maxillary and mandibular dental arches and congenital absence of some teeth. Which of the following is the most likely trinucleotide repeat that explains these findings?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Genetic mutation -> Trinucleotide repeat expansion -> Fragile X syndrome -> CGG repeat -> 95%
CHAIN: Trinucleotide repeat expansion -> Neurological symptoms and intellectual disability -> Fragile X syndrome -> CGG repeat -> 90%
CHAIN: CGG repeat -> Fragile X syndrome -> Clinical features such as elongated face, large forehead, prominent chin, and behavior disorders -> 85%
CHAIN: CGG repeat -> Fragile X syndrome -> Dental abnormalities including multiple teeth, crowding, and congenital absence of some teeth -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely trinucleotide repeat that explains the findings in this 14-year-old boy is the CGG repeat, associated with Fragile X syndrome. This repeat expansion leads to neurological symptoms, intellectual disability, behavior disorders with autistic features, elongated face, large forehead, prominent chin, and dental abnormalities including multiple teeth, crowding, and congenital absence of some teeth. The evidence paths support the link between Fragile X syndrome and the clinical manifestations observed in the patient.
analysis: The core medical principle here is to recognize the clinical features associated with Fragile X syndrome, which include neurological symptoms, intellectual disability, behavior disorders with autistic features, elongated face, large forehead, prominent chin, and dental abnormalities. The trinucleotide repeat most commonly associated with Fragile X syndrome is the CGG repeat. Given the patient's presentation of multiple teeth with crowding, congenital absence of some teeth, and other characteristic features, the most likely correct option is CGG.
